Julian of Eclanum
jū´lĭ-an ŏv ĕk´la-nŭm
n. (Julian of Eclanum, c. 386–455, bishop of Eclanum in Apulia, the ablest defender of Pelagianism and Augustine's antagonist for twenty years)
Latin Julianus; Eclanum was a town of the Hirpini in southern Italy. Not Julian the Apostate, the emperor.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Julian of Eclanum was the son of a bishop, married in a wedding Paulinus of Nola celebrated in verse, and made bishop young. When Pelagianism was condemned he refused to subscribe, lost his see, and spent the rest of his life writing against Augustine, who answered him at enormous length in the unfinished Opus Imperfectum. Julian is the clearest of the Pelagians because he argued the premises openly. He held that Adam's sin injured only Adam; that infants are born in the state Adam was created in; that concupiscence is a natural good, part of the body God made; and that death is a condition of nature, not a penalty. He accused Augustine of Manichaeism for teaching otherwise, which was a shrewd charge against a former Manichee and a false one. Scripture decides it. “Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men” (Rom 5:12) makes Adam's act the entry of both sin and death for all. Psa 51:5 traces it to conception, Eph 2:3 calls us “by nature the children of wrath,” and Job 14:4 asks what Julian never answered: “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines original sin, in theology, as the sin which is imputed to all men in consequence of the fall and transgression of Adam.

expand to see more

ORIG'INAL, a. First in order; preceding all others.

ORIGINAL SIN, in theology, that sin which is imputed to all men, with its corruption of nature, in consequence of the fall and first transgression of Adam.

DEPRAV'ITY, n. A vitiated state; corruption of moral principles.

Key Scripture

Rom 5:12 — "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:"

Psa 51:5 — "Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me."

Eph 2:3 — "Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others."

Job 14:4 — "Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one."

Modern Corruption

Julian is more modern than Augustine: his doctrine of the newborn child, of desire and of death is what most people in the West now assume without having read a word of him.

expand to see more

Pelagianism was condemned and then quietly won the popular mind. Julian's three theses — that children are born innocent, that desire is simply natural, and that death belongs to the constitution of things — are the default convictions of the modern West, including much of the evangelical West, and they are held without argument because they feel obvious. Scripture contradicts each. Psa 51:5 says “I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me,” which is a statement about origin, not about an unhappy childhood. Rom 5:12 makes death a wage. The doctrine of original sin is not a gloomy opinion about children; it is the reason the gospel must be monergistic.

The second corruption is the therapeutic reframing of Augustine's doctrine as damage to self-worth, so that the charge against him is now psychological rather than exegetical. That is Julian's charge in a new dress and it fails for the same reason: the question is not whether the doctrine is pleasant but whether Rom 5:12 and Eph 2:3 say it. They do. And the doctrine is in fact the only ground of comfort available, since a man who is “by nature” a child of wrath is saved by sovereign mercy and not by a capacity he was supposed to have and cannot find.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hamartia (G266), sin; physis (G5449), nature; Hebrew chul (H2342), to be brought forth; tame (H2931), unclean.

Greek hamartia (G266) — sin, a missing of the mark; Romans 5:12.

Greek physis (G5449) — nature, native condition; Ephesians 2:3.

Greek orge (G3709) — wrath, settled indignation; Ephesians 2:3.

Hebrew avon (H5771) — iniquity, perversity; Psalm 51:5.

Hebrew tame (H2931) — unclean, defiled; Job 14:4.

Usage

"“as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin” (Rom 5:12) — the verse his system had to evade."

"“I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5) — against the innocent newborn."

"“Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one” (Job 14:4) — the question he never answered."
